newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky stays to make sure of new Albania deal.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky stays to make sure of new Albania deal.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday he had persuaded Albanian political parties to compromise over new elections and unexpectedly extended his stay in the country to make sure the agreement was respected.

Vranitzky warned that the eyes of the international community were on Albania. His spokeswoman later said he would stay as his presence was seen as "indispensable" to make sure the agreement went through.
The elections are seen as key to avert a new crisis in the Balkan state after it was plunged into riots and violence in February and March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
"The Albanian people and the international community are increasingly concerned with the hesitant attitude...to move ahead with the elections on a cross-party basis," he said.
"We have emphasized that free and fair elections are the only solution to the continued political, economic and security crisis facing Albania," he added.
Vranitzky told a news conference he had convinced the parties to amend a new electoral law, which had caused most political parties to threaten to boycott the planned elections.
He was to extend his stay in the country overnight to make sure the parties carry out the planned amendments and make an electoral law that was acceptable to all.
It was Vranitzky's fifth trip to Albania, the latest only last week, since the troubles began.
Most parties threatened to boycott the poll after the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha forced a law through parliament which the parties said favoured Berisha.

Vranitzky said the electoral law would be brought back to parliament on Thursday evening. He also said that an election law prepared by an interim Government of National Reconciliation would also be discussed.

He said that if the compromise was not respected the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the Council of Europe and other international bodies would reconsider their commitment to monitor the elections, vital for them to be considered as free and fair.
